blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State what a trade union is, and identify the features that distinguish it from other organisations in the economy.

blocks.heading: The definition
blocks.text: A trade union is an organisation of workers, joined and funded by them, that aims to protect and improve its members' pay and working conditions. Membership is normally voluntary: a worker who joins pays a subscription, and the money pays the union's organisers and offices. The point of joining is strength in numbers. One cleaner asking alone for a higher rate carries little weight, whereas a union speaking for all the cleaners at once puts the case for all of them together. Unions usually organise by trade or by workplace, so their members share an employer or a type of work.

blocks.heading: Two unions, two countries
blocks.text: At Oshakati Textiles, the machinists belong to the Textile Workers' Union, which negotiates their hourly rate with the firm each year. In Japan, workers at an electronics assembly plant in Nagoya belong to a plant union of the same kind: members pay a subscription, elect their organisers, and the union bargains with the plant's management over pay and holidays. Different economies, same shape - organisations of workers, funded by subscriptions, acting for members' pay and conditions.

blocks.heading: Not everything with trade in it is a union
blocks.text: Do not let the word trade mislead you. A trade union has no link to trade between nations, the buying and selling of goods across borders taught elsewhere in the syllabus. The test is membership and purpose: a trade union's members are workers, and it bargains with employers over pay and conditions; a body that promotes a country's exports has firms or the government behind it and does not bargain for anyone's wages.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: This topic builds on workers and their reward, taught in topic 3.3, and sits beside firms, taught in topic 3.5, whose side of the bargaining table this topic returns to. The government's part in labour matters is taught in topic 4.1.
